definition: Wolfram Mathematica (also known as Mathematica) is a software system with built-in libraries for several areas of technical computing that allows machine learning, statistics, symbolic computation, data manipulation, network analysis, time series analysis, quantum computation framework, NLP, optimization, plotting functions and various types of data, implementation of algorithms, creation of user interfaces, and interfacing with programs written in other programming languages.
details: It was conceived by Stephen Wolfram, and is developed by Wolfram Research of Champaign, Illinois. The Wolfram Language is the programming language used in Mathematica. Mathematica 1.0 was released on June 23, 1988 in Champaign, Illinois and Santa Clara, California. Mathematica's Wolfram Language is fundamentally based on Lisp.

explainer.lead: Wolfram Mathematica is a software system with built-in libraries spanning technical computing, including machine learning, statistics, symbolic computation and much more. It matters as a broad environment for computation, algorithms and interfaces.

tiers.eli5: It's a big toolbox for doing maths with symbols as well as numbers, plus charts, data work and programming, all in one program.
tiers.practitioner: Users write in the Wolfram Language to do symbolic computation, data manipulation, plotting and interfacing with other languages. A pitfall is forgetting that the Wolfram Language is fundamentally based on Lisp, which shapes how code is structured.
tiers.paperLevel: A software system with built-in libraries for technical computing areas including machine learning, statistics, symbolic computation, data manipulation, network analysis, time series analysis, quantum computation, NLP and optimisation; it is programmed in the Wolfram Language, fundamentally based on Lisp.

explainer.example: A user performs symbolic computation and plots the results in one system, then interfaces with a program written in another programming language.
